results.reader_more: Delphi panels are used routinely in foresight, but their forecasts are seldom audited once the forecast period has passed. This study does that audit in the drugs field, comparing predictions made by an expert Delphi against what subsequently happened. Accuracy turns out to be uneven: some predicted developments materialised, others did not, and the pattern is informative about where expert consensus is trustworthy and where it is not. Because the object of study is the method rather than the drug trends themselves, the findings transfer to other domains that rely on Delphi. The authors are appropriately cautious about generalising from a single retrospective comparison.

results.reader_title: Why strong European science does not convert into academic spin-offs
results.reader_what: Weak commercialisation stems from functional misalignment between innovation systems and entrepreneurial ecosystems, not resource scarcity.
results.reader_why: Adding more support instruments will not help if governance functions remain misaligned.
results.reader_more: Europe publishes strongly but turns comparatively little public research into companies. Building on the Knowledge Spillover Theory of Entrepreneurship, this paper reads that gap as a knowledge filter problem caused by misalignment between innovation systems and entrepreneurial ecosystems. It defines alignment as a governance condition spanning structural, functional and resource domains, and uses the Triple Helix Twin model to place regional public actors as the orchestrators. Empirically it examines academic spin-offs across seven European regions, identifying recurring tensions and governance archetypes. The key finding is that weak commercialisation comes less from structural constraints or lack of money than from functional misalignment — so adding instruments without integrating governance will not fix it.
